affirm

uh-FURM -- two syllables, stress on the second syllable, FURM. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To affirm is to state something as a fact.

The spokesperson affirmed that the concert would go on despite the storm forecast.

Example

By lunchtime, the whole seventh grade 'knows' the pool will be closed all summer -- somebody's cousin heard it somewhere. Then the intercom crackles: 'To put the rumors to rest,' the principal says, 'I can affirm that the pool opens June first, right on schedule.'

The principal affirms the fact: she states it firmly, publicly, and on her own authority, cutting through the swirl of rumor. That is affirm's job -- not arguing, not guessing, but planting a statement as fact and standing behind it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

avow: To avow is to state something openly that others might hide -- a belief, a loyalty, a mistake. Avowing is personal and a little brave, admitting where you stand. To affirm is cooler and more public: stating a fact as true on your own authority, with nothing confessed.

maintain: To maintain a claim is to keep asserting it over time, especially when others push back -- persistence is the point. To affirm is a single, calm act: one clear statement of fact, made once and stood behind.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deny: to say that something is not true

dispute: to argue against a claim

Where it sits · how much doubt it removes

declare → affirm → confirm

declare vs. affirm: Declare sits below affirm: to declare just puts a statement on the record, loudly and publicly, whatever its evidence, while to affirm is to add your own authority and stand behind the statement as fact.

confirm vs. affirm: Confirm is the strongest: to affirm is to stand behind a statement as fact, but to confirm is to settle the question entirely -- once something is confirmed, the doubting is over.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — af-: to, toward (a form of ad-) (Latin)

root — firm-: strong, steadfast (Latin firmus 'firm, strong')

Put it together: Affirm is Latin affirmare: ad- ('to') plus firmare ('to make firm'), from firmus, 'strong.' To affirm something is literally to make it firm -- to take a wobbly, rumored, doubted statement and plant it solidly as fact. The firmness in the word is the speaker's own: whoever affirms is holding the statement steady.

Use the root in a new word: infirmary: The campus map shows the infirmary at the end of the east hall.

Root Check

Word Choice

Affirm almost always takes that plus a full statement: officials affirm that the water is safe, doctors affirm that the runner is fit. It is calm and declarative -- no shouting, no arguing, just a fact stated and stood behind. Keep it apart from its unit-mate allege: to allege is to raise an unproven claim of wrongdoing, while to affirm is to state something as settled fact on your own authority.
